scenario: A young adult has unexplained syncope during a febrile illness. Interpret the right-precordial leads and AV conduction.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: Coved ST elevation with subsequent T-wave inversion in the right-precordial leads is a type 1 Brugada pattern. The source also documents first-degree AV block. A Brugada pattern requires clinical assessment before labeling the syndrome.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Confirm lead placement and repeat right-precordial leads at standard and higher intercostal positions when indicated. Review fever, drugs, electrolytes, syncope and family history. Obtain specialist electrophysiology assessment; distinguish a Brugada ECG pattern from the clinical syndrome.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Treat fever promptly and avoid recognized provoking drugs. Arrange monitored urgent care for arrhythmic syncope or ventricular arrhythmia. ICD decisions depend on clinical risk, not the tracing alone. Counsel regarding family assessment and specialist follow-up.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: T-wave flattening, ST depression and prominent U-wave activity support hypokalemia in this setting. Measure QT carefully and avoid including the U wave as the T-wave endpoint.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Measure potassium, magnesium, renal function and acid-base status. Review GI losses, diuretics and other drugs. Monitor rhythm; repeat ECG and electrolytes during replacement. Distinguish a prominent U wave from the end of the T wave.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Replace potassium with a route and rate appropriate to severity, symptoms, renal function and ECG findings. Severe or symptomatic cases require monitored IV replacement using local safety protocols; never give IV potassium as a bolus. Correct magnesium deficiency and ongoing losses. QT/QU prolongation increases arrhythmic risk.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: Short PR and slurred initial QRS upstroke support ventricular pre-excitation (WPW pattern). The rhythm shown is not pre-excited AF. Symptoms determine whether this represents WPW syndrome.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Repeat a full 12-lead ECG, obtain previous tracings, echocardiography and ambulatory rhythm monitoring. Refer for electrophysiology assessment and accessory-pathway risk stratification.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Arrange cardiology/electrophysiology review; catheter ablation can provide definitive treatment in symptomatic patients. If a rapid irregular broad-complex rhythm develops, suspect pre-excited AF: avoid AV-nodal blockers, including adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin and IV amiodarone. Unstable patients require urgent electrical cardioversion; stable cases require specialist-directed therapy.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: A sustained broad-complex tachycardia is highly concerning for ventricular tachycardia. The clinical tracing is labeled VT by its source. Management depends immediately on pulse and hemodynamic stability.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Immediately assess pulse and stability. Obtain a 12-lead ECG if it does not delay treatment, continuous monitoring, electrolytes and assessment for ischemia or structural disease. Look for AV dissociation and capture/fusion beats where visible.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Treat an uncertain broad-complex tachycardia as VT. Pulseless VT requires CPR and defibrillation; unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse requires synchronized cardioversion. Stable sustained VT needs monitored expert management, with cardioversion or antiarrhythmic treatment selected for the clinical context. Avoid empiric verapamil in undifferentiated broad-complex tachycardia.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: An S1Q3T3 pattern is a right-heart strain clue compatible with PE. This pattern is neither sensitive nor specific. The diagnosis requires integration with clinical probability and appropriate imaging.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Assess clinical probability and hemodynamic stability. Use CTPA when appropriate; D-dimer is useful in selected low/intermediate-probability presentations. Bedside echocardiography can guide urgent care when unstable and transport is unsafe. Assess troponin, renal function and bleeding risk.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Provide monitored supportive care and anticoagulation when indicated, considering bleeding risk and diagnostic certainty. Shock from high-risk PE requires urgent specialist assessment for reperfusion. An ECG cannot confirm PE or determine clot burden; absence of right-heart strain does not exclude it.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: QT prolongation suggests delayed ventricular repolarization and torsades risk. The source tracing illustrates prolonged QT but does not establish sotalol exposure in the source patient. Verify QT manually; the printed tracing uses 50 mm/s, so use its own calibration.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Manually assess QT and rate correction using the printed speed; review drugs, renal function and potassium, magnesium and calcium. Obtain serial ECGs and continuous monitoring when clinically significant. Consider congenital disease if prolongation persists.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Stop QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolytes. With suspected sotalol accumulation, obtain urgent toxicology/cardiology advice and account for renal impairment. Torsades requires IV magnesium and immediate defibrillation for sustained unstable polymorphic VT or arrest; recurrent pause-dependent acquired torsades may need rate acceleration under specialist supervision.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: A widespread ST-elevation pattern is compatible with pericarditis in this clinical setting. Compare with early repolarization and STEMI. Symptoms, examination, biomarkers and echocardiography help establish the diagnosis.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Assess hemodynamics, inflammatory markers, troponin, renal function and echocardiography for effusion and ventricular dysfunction. Evaluate infectious and systemic causes according to history. Exclude ACS where appropriate.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Treat confirmed uncomplicated inflammatory pericarditis with an appropriate anti-inflammatory regimen and colchicine when suitable, with gastroprotection and activity advice. Admit high-risk patients, including those with fever, a large effusion, tamponade or myocardial involvement. A compatible ECG alone is insufficient to diagnose pericarditis.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: Prominent deflections at the QRS-ST junction are Osborn J waves, compatible with hypothermia in this setting. They are not specific and must be interpreted with core temperature and clinical findings.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Measure core temperature with a suitable low-reading thermometer; assess glucose, blood gas, electrolytes and coagulation. Monitor rhythm and investigate infection, endocrine disease, intoxication or trauma as appropriate.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Handle gently, prevent further heat loss and rewarm according to severity. Use warmed supportive treatment and involve critical care. Marked instability or arrest requires a hypothermia-specific resuscitation pathway and consideration of extracorporeal rewarming. Bradycardia may improve with rewarming; treat the patient rather than an isolated rate.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: A widened QRS with a terminal right-precordial R-prime and broad terminal S waves in lateral leads supports right bundle branch block. Compare earlier tracings and assess symptoms before deciding clinical significance.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Compare prior ECGs; assess symptoms and obtain echocardiography when structural disease is suspected. In acute chest pain or breathlessness, investigate ACS or PE according to clinical probability rather than attributing symptoms to the conduction pattern.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: An isolated chronic RBBB does not automatically require a pacemaker. Treat the underlying condition. Syncope, additional fascicular disease or evidence of advanced AV block warrants urgent rhythm evaluation and possible pacing.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: This strip demonstrates polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS envelope, consistent with torsades when preceding QT prolongation is present. Assess the patient and pulse immediately; do not delay resuscitation to complete ECG measurements.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Check pulse and hemodynamics immediately. Review the preceding QT interval, drugs and potassium/magnesium/calcium. Identify bradycardia, pauses, ischemia and reversible triggers.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Sustained unstable polymorphic VT or pulseless VT requires immediate unsynchronized defibrillation, with CPR if pulseless. Give IV magnesium for torsades, stop QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolytes. Recurrent acquired pause-dependent episodes may require pacing or specialist-directed rate acceleration. Avoid QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: The ECG is consistent with third-degree AV block with an escape rhythm. Establish the atrial and ventricular rates independently, assess QRS width and determine whether there are signs of poor perfusion.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Continuous cardiac monitoring, serial 12-lead ECGs and rhythm strips; review AV-nodal blocking drugs, ischemia, electrolytes and reversible causes. Obtain echocardiography and urgent cardiology review for symptomatic or advanced block.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Assess for shock, syncope, ischemia and heart failure. Prepare pacing early in unstable high-grade AV block; transcutaneous pacing may bridge to transvenous pacing. Drug treatment depends on the rhythm and local bradycardia protocol; atropine is unreliable in infranodal block. Persistent advanced block without a reversible cause may require permanent pacing.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: The anterior ST-depression pattern with prominent anterior R waves raises concern for posterior myocardial infarction. Obtain V7-V9 posterior leads and activate the appropriate acute occlusion pathway when supported by the clinical assessment.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Obtain serial ECGs, troponin, electrolytes and urgent cardiology assessment. Assess hemodynamics and complications; use echocardiography when helpful without delaying reperfusion. Additional right-sided or posterior leads may clarify the territory.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Activate the acute coronary syndrome/reperfusion pathway for ongoing ischemia with diagnostic acute occlusion findings. Give antithrombotic treatment as appropriate after contraindication assessment and according to local protocol. Do not wait for troponin to arrange reperfusion. Monitor for arrhythmia and shock; oxygen is indicated for hypoxemia, not routinely.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: Loss of visible P waves with tall T waves may occur with severe hyperkalemia and sinoventricular conduction. This is an annotated teaching strip, not a complete 12-lead ECG. Do not diagnose atrial fibrillation solely because P waves are absent.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Obtain urgent potassium, blood gas, glucose, renal function, calcium and magnesium; repeat a hemolyzed specimen without delaying treatment when ECG toxicity is present. Start continuous monitoring and review drugs and dialysis history.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Urgently stabilize the myocardium with IV calcium when hyperkalemic ECG changes are present. Shift potassium intracellularly with insulin and glucose with serial glucose monitoring; nebulized beta-agonist is an adjunct. Remove potassium and correct the cause; arrange urgent dialysis when indicated. Recheck potassium for rebound. Calcium does not lower potassium.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: Grouped beats with missing P waves suggest sinus arrest or sinoatrial exit block. This supports possible sinus-node dysfunction when symptoms correlate. Distinguish missing atrial impulses from AV block, in which P waves continue.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Correlate symptoms with telemetry or ambulatory monitoring. Review drugs, ischemia, thyroid function and electrolytes. Inspect whether P waves disappear during pauses and whether pause duration suggests exit block; one short strip may not distinguish all mechanisms.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Treat unstable symptomatic bradycardia with urgent monitored support and pacing when required. Correct reversible causes. Persistent symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction can require a permanent pacemaker after symptom-rhythm correlation; a pause alone is not a complete clinical diagnosis.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: The extract illustrates shortened repolarization and abnormal ST morphology associated with hypercalcemia. It shows V1-V3 only; confirm intervals on a full calibrated ECG and measure calcium. ST changes may mimic acute ischemia.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Confirm ionized or albumin-adjusted calcium, renal function, phosphate, magnesium and PTH. Review calcium/vitamin D supplements and drugs; investigate malignancy or other causes according to PTH and history.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: For significant symptomatic hypercalcemia, restore volume with carefully monitored isotonic fluid when appropriate and stop contributory agents. Arrange cause-specific calcium-lowering treatment with specialist input, accounting for renal and cardiac function. Monitor ECG and electrolytes. A short QT is a clue, not a substitute for calcium measurement.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?

questions.answer: Urgently cardiovert if the rhythm causes hemodynamic instability. In stable patients, choose rate or rhythm control with cardiology input. questions.answer: The source documents combined hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia. Peaked T waves support hyperkalemia, while hypocalcemia can prolong the ST/QT interval. A mixed disturbance may not follow the textbook appearance of either abnormality alone.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Obtain urgent potassium, blood gas, glucose, renal function, calcium and magnesium; repeat a hemolyzed specimen without delaying treatment when ECG toxicity is present. Start continuous monitoring and review drugs and dialysis history.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Urgently stabilize the myocardium with IV calcium when hyperkalemic ECG changes are present. Shift potassium intracellularly with insulin and glucose with serial glucose monitoring; nebulized beta-agonist is an adjunct. Remove potassium and correct the cause; arrange urgent dialysis when indicated. Recheck potassium for rebound. Calcium does not lower potassium.

questions.question: Describe the ECG and give the most likely interpretation.
questions.answer: Sinus tachycardia and a right bundle branch block pattern can accompany acute right ventricular strain. The source patient had PE; the ECG alone cannot confirm PE in a new patient.

questions.question: Which assessments and investigations are required?
questions.answer: Assess clinical probability and hemodynamic stability. Use CTPA when appropriate; D-dimer is useful in selected low/intermediate-probability presentations. Bedside echocardiography can guide urgent care when unstable and transport is unsafe. Assess troponin, renal function and bleeding risk.

questions.question: How would you manage this clinical presentation?
questions.answer: Provide monitored supportive care and anticoagulation when indicated, considering bleeding risk and diagnostic certainty. Shock from high-risk PE requires urgent specialist assessment for reperfusion. An ECG cannot confirm PE or determine clot burden; absence of right-heart strain does not exclude it.
